title: Hotter than the Sun: fusion's record year - and its biggest catch
dek: Machines in the US and South Korea broke temperature and time records in 2026. None has yet made more power than it uses.

article: Fusion, the process that powers the Sun, has been called the energy source of the future for decades. In 2026 a string of records suggested that future may be edging closer, but the hardest test has still not been passed.

Fusion works by forcing the nuclei of light atoms to merge. Most machines use two forms, or isotopes, of hydrogen: deuterium, which has one neutron, and tritium, which has two. When they fuse, they form helium and release a neutron carrying a great deal of energy. Because nuclei repel each other, the fuel must be heated into a plasma - a gas so hot that electrons are stripped from their atoms.
How hot? About 100 million °C is widely regarded as the threshold for a commercially useful machine, roughly seven times the temperature at the centre of the Sun.

In February, Helion, a US start-up, said its Polaris prototype had reached 150 million °C and had become the first privately built machine to produce measurable fusion with deuterium-tritium fuel. Helion has agreed to supply electricity to Microsoft from a power plant it hopes to switch on by 2028.

Months later, South Korea's KSTAR reactor held plasma at 100 million °C for 102 seconds, more than double its record of 48 seconds from 2024. Engineers credit a new lining of tungsten, a metal with an exceptionally high melting point, in the part of the machine that handles the plasma's exhaust heat.

Yet temperature and duration are not the same as useful power. Helion did not say how much fusion Polaris produced, and its 2028 timeline has not been independently confirmed. No fusion machine has yet produced more electricity than it consumes - the milestone any power station would need.

There are chemical hurdles, too. Tritium is radioactive and extremely rare in nature, so future plants would need to produce their own supply, and the walls of a reactor must survive years of bombardment by fast neutrons.

Investors are betting anyway: fusion companies raised a record $4.5 billion over the past year, a 69% jump. Whether that money can buy a working power plant this decade remains the field's biggest open question.

tasks.q: Which headline best sums up the WHOLE article?
options: Fusion set new records in 2026, but no machine yet makes more power than it uses
Fusion power plants now supply Microsoft with electricity
Tungsten has an exceptionally high melting point
Scientists prove that fusion energy is impossible
tasks.explain: B distorts paragraph 4 (2028 is only a hope). C is one detail from paragraph 5. D contradicts the whole article. A combines the records (paragraphs 4-5) with the catch (paragraph 6).

tasks.q: Put the steps of fusion in order (paragraph 2).
items: Hydrogen fuel is heated to extreme temperatures
Electrons are stripped away, forming a plasma
Deuterium and tritium nuclei collide and merge
Helium forms and a fast neutron is released
tasks.explain: Heating comes first because the positively charged nuclei repel each other - only very fast-moving nuclei can get close enough to fuse.

tasks.q: Scan the article: what does each figure refer to?

pairs.right: threshold for a commercially useful machine
when Helion hopes to switch on a power plant
raised by fusion companies in the past year

tasks.explain: Two temperatures and two times appear close together - check which machine and which year each belongs to.

statements.text: Tritium has more neutrons than deuterium.
statements.explain: Paragraph 2: deuterium has one neutron, tritium has two.

statements.text: Helion's Polaris already supplies electricity to Microsoft.
statements.explain: Paragraph 4: Helion only hopes to switch on a power plant by 2028.

statements.text: KSTAR used deuterium-tritium fuel in its record run.
statements.explain: Paragraph 5 never says what fuel KSTAR used.

statements.text: Some fusion machines already produce more electricity than they consume.
statements.explain: Paragraph 6: "No fusion machine has yet" done this.

statements.text: Tungsten is cheaper than other metals used in reactors.
statements.explain: Paragraph 5 mentions tungsten's melting point, not its price.

tasks.q: Why might readers treat Helion's announcement with some caution?
options: It did not say how much fusion occurred, and its timeline is not independently confirmed
It used a fuel that cannot fuse
tasks.explain: Paragraph 6 gives both reasons. B misreads the numbers (it was 150 million °C); C and D are never said.

tasks.q: In paragraph 3, "threshold" is closest in meaning to:
options: the level that must be reached
tasks.explain: A machine below 100 million °C is not commercially useful; at or above it, it might be. D is the literal meaning (a doorway), which does not fit here.

tasks.q: What does paragraph 7 add to the argument?
options: A different kind of obstacle, beyond reaching high temperatures for long enough
More evidence that fusion is nearly ready
A description of how Helion's machine works
The reasons investors are leaving the field
tasks.explain: "There are chemical hurdles, too" - the word "too" signals an additional problem: fuel supply and wall materials.

write.prompt: Should governments spend more on fusion research, or on energy that already works, such as solar power? Write 2-3 sentences in English and give one reason.
write.sample: I think governments should keep funding fusion, but not at the expense of solar power. Fusion has passed an important threshold in temperature, yet no machine has produced more electricity than it consumes, so we still need energy that works today.
